full_judgment:
16. Now the pertinent question that calls for determination is who caused such injuries which resulted in the death. Section 106 of the Evidence Act speaks about the burden of proving the fact especially within the knowledge of any person. It reads as follows: 

 "106.Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge, when any fact is especially within knowledge of any person the burden of proving that fact is upon him." 

 Although prosecution is saddled with the burden of proving the case to its entirety, section 106 of the Evidence Act is an exception to the general rule and also to section 101 of the Evidence Act. Section 106 lays down that any fact which is within the knowledge of any person, that person alone is to discharge the onus of proving that fact. For instance: A was taken to the house of B. A was subsequently found dead with injuries on his person. The character and circumstances of the death of A suggest that B killed A. B is therefore required to rebut the presumption that he is not responsible for killing A. B is furthered required to prove the nature and cause of 'A's death. Where the subject matter of the allegation lies peculiarly within the knowledge of one of the parties, that party must prove it. When a person does an act with some intention other than that which the character and circumstance of the case suggest, it is not for the prosecution to eliminate all other possible intentions. If the accused had a different intention, that is a fact especially within his knowledge. He is to prove such special knowledge on fact. 

 18. In this case a peculiar or startling phenomenon exists if the burden of proof shifts on the accused to prove his innocence. Or, in other words, if he is required to prove that he did not commit murder. This is not the intention of section 106 of the Evidence Act. If knowledge of certain facts is as much available to the prosecution, prosecution must choose to exercise such diligence in order to obtain that knowledge as provisions of section 101 have not been made nugatory by section 106 of the Evidence Act. 

 19. In the instant case, the deceased Awal was found dead in the courtyard of the accused. So, it is within their special knowledge to explain the cause of death. The accused persons are therefore saddled with the burden of proving the factum of death of Awal, but section 106 of the Evidence Act does not totally absolve the prosecution from its duty of proving the fact. The crime although committed within the special knowledge of the accused, the prosecution owes a duty to prove the same. In this case when the deceased was taken out from his house to the house of accused and he is found dead with multiple injuries on his persons in the verandah of the accused persons, it is the accused and accused alone who are to account for this. In our view provision of section 106 of the Evidence Act attracts in this case. As we have already found that the intention of taking away Awal by the accused persons has not been to cause murder but he was taken out of his house with the purpose of effecting a divorce of his second wife by Awal and in the process of effecting such divorce, the accused appears to have taken resort to perpetrate torture which eventually might have resulted in death of Awal. As there is a marital relationship between Awal and the accused persons and Awal having married Anwara Begum @ Angur Begum, the sister of the accused Selim, Shahjahan, Halim and son-in-law of Lokman and Maleka Bibi and further that Awal having 3 children out of the wedlock with Angur, the accused persons did not appear to have intended to kill him; because by such killing Anwara would be rendered widow and further the burden of maintenance of the orphan children would eventually fall upon the accused persons. Apart from this aspect, if the accused persons had really intended to kill Awal, they could drag him to a jungle or in an isolated place where the dead body could not be traced out or no witness could be available. Further the dead body of Awal was found in the verandah of the accused persons which indicates that the accused did not attempt to cause the disappearance of the dead body. Therefore the motive for killing, in our view, is a remote one but as we have already observed that to effect the divorce of the second wife of Awal, the accused persons might have given a serious beating which resulted in his death. Therefore, the offence committed by the accused persons, in our view, does not attract the provision of section 302 read with section 109 of the Penal Code. The injury so found on the dead body of Awal, in the natural course, has resulted in the death but at least the accused had the knowledge that such injury might result in death. Therefore, the offence committed by the accused, in our view, would attract the provision of section 304 Part II of the Penal Code. We have already seen from the information lodged by Iman Ali Sheikh on 10.1.91 that accused Manik, Selim, Maleka and Anwara went to the house of Awal and took away Awal along with them. Accused Maleka has been acquitted by the learned Additional Sessions Judge. From the conduct of accused Anwara Begum @ Angur Begum it appears that she might not have inflicted any injury while Awal was taken to their house or from the conduct of Anwara it cannot be suggested that she had the complicity to kill Awal. Therefore, in our view, the charge under section 302 as levelled against Anwara Begum @ Angur Begum falls through. She is thus acquitted of the charge levelled against her.
